# Executive Summary

SEPA’s current flood models assume that an extreme river flow event has a fixed shape, which is only varied by its maximum flow. Its flood inundation models are computationally expensive and time consuming, so they use simpler statistical models (emulators) to approximate the results of the inundation models. These models use hydrographs, graphs showing how river flow changes over a period of extreme flow, as inputs. 

Unlike the current models, we examined the whole event, including aspects of the overall shape in addition to its peak. We used `r n_years` years of data from the River Don at Parkhill gauging station and identified `r N_events` extreme flow events. Using these events, we compared SEPA’s approach to five other methods of describing hydrograph shapes: polynomial regression, principal component analysis (PCA), wavelets, B-splines and a gamma-type function. As emulators favour fewer parameters, we also evaluated how well each method reproduced the event hydrographs with as few parameters as possible.

PCA and wavelets were the most promising, reducing the reconstruction error from `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ with SEPA’s approach to `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_wav)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ respectively. Our chosen PCA setting requires `r S("PCA", "inputs")` emulator inputs compared to `r S("Wavelets", "inputs")` for the wavelet model, reducing the number of inundation model runs considerably, and at this level it still explains 95\% of the observed variation in shape.

We recommend SEPA adopts PCA and uses a conditional smoothed bootstrap method to simulate new hydrograph shapes, this reuses the variation seen in past events and adjusts the size and timing to the new event. SEPA’s approach on average miscalculated the volume of water by `r sprintf("%.0f", S("SEPA (average shape)", "volume_out"))`\% and gave a single volume of `r sprintf("%.1f", volume_table$median[1])` million m$^3$ for an event of median size and timing, whereas 90\% of our simulated shapes gives a range between  `r sprintf("%.1f", pca_boot_volume$lower)` and `r sprintf("%.1f", pca_boot_volume$upper)` million m$^3$.

Our recommendation does have limitations, including that it does not fully reproduce unusual events, such as multi-peaks, and its simulated 90\% ranges contain only `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "coverage"))`\% of all observed flows. Despite this, when combined with an emulator, a PCA method lets SEPA explore a wider range of plausible extreme flow events, supporting better informed decisions on flood risk. 

# Data and Exploratory Data Analysis {#initial-analysis}

We have extended the 15-minute discharge data for the River Don at Parkhill from ten [water years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_year) in Part 1 to twenty-five for Part 2. Years were formatted into water years to reflect the seasonality of river flows as recommended in Robson and Reed [-@robson1999]. We retain the 65 $m^3/s$ threshold and the Robson and Reed [-@robson1999] independence criteria, which identify `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events, an average of `r sprintf("%.2f", nrow(peaks) / n_years)` per year.

### Suspect readings {#suspect-readings}

SEPA flags `r format(n_suspect, big.mark = ",")` readings (`r sprintf("%.2f", pct_suspect)`% of the record) as Suspect (code 150), meaning that the flow lies beyond the acceptable extrapolation limit of the gauge's stage-discharge relationship. None of these exceed the `r u_final` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ threshold, with the largest being `r sprintf("%.1f", max_suspect)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, or lie within the 118 event windows. Hence, we continue to exclude these readings.

## Standardising the hydrographs {#standardising-the-hydrographs}

To separate these parameters and isolate each hydrograph's shape, we standardise the events. We denote peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, duration $W_i$, and relative peak position $\tau_i$, and do so as follows:

- Each event is defined between its rising trough, last reading within 5\% of the minimum flow in the 7 days before the peak, and falling limb trough, first reading within 5\% of the minimum flow in the 7 days after it, or the next peak if this occurs first.

- Time is rescaled to the interval [0,1], with zero and one representing the start and end of the event, respectively.

- Relative peak position is calculated as $\tau_i = \frac{t_i^{\text{peak}} - t_i^{\text{start}}}{W_i}$.

- Rising and falling limbs are rescaled separately to align all hydrograph peaks at the mean relative peak position, $u^* =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", u_star)`.

- Discharge is divided by maximum flow $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, standardising hydrograph peaks to have value of one.

- Hydrographs are evaluated at 64 equally spaced points on the standardised time scale by linear interpolation.

- The resulting data are arranged into a matrix ($Y$), with one row per event and 64 columns, one for each time point.

Alongside these, we retain peak discharge, event duration and relative peak position separately, allowing for standardisation to be reversed.

```{r standardised-curves, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap=paste0("Each step of the standardisation, where the red dashed lines are the common peak position $u^*$ and the bold line is the mean of the standardised hydrographs.")}
standardised_curves_plot
```

# Methods for representing hydrograph shape
Each standardised event (Section \@ref(standardising-the-hydrographs)) then comprises `r n_grid` discharge values, peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, duration $W_i$, and relative peak position $\tau_i$. To reduce the number of emulator inputs, we investigate five different methods: polynomial regression, principal component analysis (PCA), wavelets, B-splines and a gamma-type function.

In most of the methods, each standardised hydrograph is represented by a weighted sum of $K$ basis functions,

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_{ik}\,\phi_k(u),
(\#eq:basis)
\end{equation}

where $\phi_k(u)$ are the basis functions and $\theta_{ik}$ are the shape parameters for event $i$. The methods mainly differ in how these functions are chosen, but the exceptions are PCA, which first subtracts the mean curve before applying \@ref(eq:basis), and the gamma-type curve, which is a nonlinear function of its parameters [@nash1957instantaneous]. Each event is then described by the emulator inputs

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{x}_i = \left(Q_i^{\text{peak}},\; W_i,\; \tau_i,\; \boldsymbol{\theta}_i\right).
(\#eq:inputs)
\end{equation}

This gives $K+3$ inputs in total, where $K$ is considerably smaller than the previous `r n_grid`.

## SEPA's approach {#method-SEPA}

Our baseline is SEPA's approach, in which each event's flow is divided by its peak flow, aligned at its peak and averaged over events in real hours $h$ from the peak,
\begin{equation}
\bar{y}(h) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{l=1}^{N} \frac{Q_l(t_l^{\text{peak}} + h)}{Q_l^{\text{peak}}},
(\#eq:sepa)
\end{equation}
and then its peak is rescaled to one. Every event then uses this single shape and scales by its peak flow, $\hat{Q}_i(t) = Q_i^{\text{peak}}\,\bar{y}(t - t_i^{\text{peak}})$.

## Evaluation criteria {#evaluation-criteria}

We compare methods on accuracy, parsimony and fitness for purpose [@wilson2026lec5], first to choose the number of parameters for the polynomial, PCA and wavelet methods (Sections \@ref(method-polynomial)-\@ref(method-wavelets)) and then in Section \@ref(Comparison).

**Accuracy:** This measures how closely each method reconstructs the observed hydrographs and it is measured by the root mean squared error (RMSE):

\begin{equation}
\text{RMSE}_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{`r n_grid`}\textstyle\sum_{j}\big(\hat{Q}_i(t_j) - Q_i(t_j)\big)^2}.
(\#eq:rmse)
\end{equation}

For the SEPA, PCA and wavelet methods, that estimate a shared basis or shape, we use leave-one-out validation to refit this representation using the remaining $N - 1$ events. On the other hand, for the polynomial, B-spline and gamma-type methods, which fit each event on its own, we report their errors in-sample because leave-one-out has no effect.

**Parsimony:** We consider the number of shape parameters used, comparing both the accuracy at different numbers, and strong correlations between parameters, which increase complexity.

**Fitness for purpose:** To understand whether the method reproduces a valid range of hydrograph shapes. We measure errors in peak discharge, peak timing and total flow volume [@wilson2026lec5]:

\begin{align}
\text{Peak error}_i &= \max_j \hat{Q}_i(t_j) - \max_j Q_i(t_j), (\#eq:peak)\\
\text{Timing error}_i &= \hat{t}_{i}^{\,\text{peak}} - t_{i}^{\,\text{peak}}, (\#eq:timing)\\
\text{Volume error}_i &= 100 \times \frac{\int \hat{Q}_i(t)\,dt - \int Q_i(t)\,dt}{\int Q_i(t)\,dt}\ \%. (\#eq:volume)
\end{align}

Since every method aligns peaks, timing errors are expected to be small by construction.

## Polynomial regression {#method-polynomial}
The first method approximates each standardised hydrograph by a polynomial of degree $p$ in time,
\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \theta_{i1}u_j + \theta_{i2}u_j^2 + \dots + \theta_{ip}u_j^p, \qquad j = 1, \dots, `r n_grid`,
(\#eq:poly)
\end{equation}
whose $p+1$ coefficients, estimated for each event by ordinary least squares,
\begin{equation}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}_i,
(\#eq:OLS)
\end{equation}
form its shape parameters, where $X$ has columns $1,u,\ldots,u^p$ and $\mathbf{y}_i$ contains the event's `r n_grid` standardised discharge values.

To choose the degree $p$, we tested degrees 2-15 and compared the errors across all events (Figure \@ref(fig:polychoice)).

## Principal component analysis (PCA) {#method-pca}

Rather than fixing the basis functions in advance, PCA estimates them from the observed hydrographs themselves [@wilson2026lec4]. After centering each column of $Y$ by subtracting the mean curve $\bar{y}(u_j)$, we take the principal components $\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots$ to be the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix, ordered by variance they explain, so that each hydrograph can be approximated by

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \bar{y}(u_j) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_{ik}\,\phi_k(u_j), \qquad \theta_{ik} = \sum_{j=1}^{`r n_grid`} \big(y_i(u_j) - \bar{y}(u_j)\big)\,\phi_k(u_j),
(\#eq:pca)
\end{equation}

where the scores $\theta_{i1}, \dots, \theta_{iK}$ are the shape parameters for event $i$. The scores are uncorrelated by construction, which simplifies uncertainty modelling.

```{r pcaloadings, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=8, fig.cap="The first three principal components $\\phi_1, \\phi_2, \\phi_3$ against standardised time.", out.width="90%", fig.align='center'}
matplot(grid_u, pca_result$rotation[, 1:3], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"),
        xlab = "Standardised time u", ylab = "Loading", main = "")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"), bty = "n")
```

From Figure \@ref(fig:pcacumvar), the first three principal components explain `r round(100 * cum_var[3])`% of the variation, and they have a physical interpretation, for example, PC1 mainly describes event width.

We select the number of parameters using the percentage of cumulative variance explained, as well as the errors in Figure \@ref(fig:pcachoice). We see that six components explain approximately 95% of the variation, and there is little improvement in leave-one-out RMSE from adding another. Hence, we select $K=6$, which reduces each hydrograph to six shape parameters.

## Wavelets {#method-wavelets}

The wavelets method represents a hydrograph using small, localised waves [@wilson2026lec4]. We applied the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to each standardised hydrograph, splitting it into a smooth component and detail components at three resolution levels:

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) = \sum_{k} a_{ik}\,\varphi_k(u) + \sum_{j=1}^{`r wav_levels`}\sum_{k} d_{ijk}\,\psi_{jk}(u),
(\#eq:wavelet)
\end{equation}

where $a_{ik}$ are the smooth coefficients and $d_{ijk}$ are the detail coefficients at scale $j$ and location $k$. 

At `r wav_levels` levels, each `r n_grid`-point hydrograph gives `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth and `r n_grid - n_grid / 2^wav_levels` detail coefficients, which allows exact reconstruction if all are retained. We choose to retain all `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth coefficients, but we select the $M$ detail coefficients with the largest mean absolute values across all events. Comparing the errors in Figure \@ref(fig:wavchoice), peak and timing error fell sharply up to $M = 5$, with little improvement after that, while RMSE decreased more gradually. Hence, we retain five detail coefficients, which gives thirteen shape parameters in total.

## Other methods {#method-other}

We considered two further methods, each addressing a weakness found above.

### B-splines {#method-bspline}

The polynomial's weaknesses stem from using a single curve across the whole event, so we introduce the B-spline method [@ramsay2005functional], which joins smaller, smooth pieces of a polynomial together, allowing for more local changes. In particular, we fitted cubic B-splines, with equally spaced knots, to each standardised event:

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \theta_{il}\,B_l(u_j)
(\#eq:bspline)
\end{equation}

where $B_l(u_j)$ are the spline basis functions and $\theta_{il}$ are estimated by least squares. In order to compare fairly with polynomial regression at a similar number of parameters, we chose $L =$ `r n_basis_chosen`, which gives `r n_basis_chosen + 1` fitted coefficients.

### Gamma-type function {#method-gamma}

Following the further reading suggested in lectures on a known function with interpretable parameters, we fit a gamma-type hydrograph [@nash1957instantaneous], with a baseflow term using nonlinear least squares. This gives three parameters with physical meaning: relative baseflow, peak timing and peak sharpness.

# Validation and comparison of methods {#Comparison}

```{r cmp-text-helpers, include = FALSE}
# Look up one value from the paired comparisons (Table 7) for the text below
pr_val <- function(comparison, metric, col) {
  paired_results[[col]][paired_results$comparison == comparison &
                          paired_results$metric == paired_metrics[[metric]]]
}
vs_sepa <- c("PCA minus SEPA (average shape)", "Wavelets minus SEPA (average shape)")
```

We now validate and compare all six approaches at their chosen number of parameters, using held-out errors in real units wherever a method learns from other events (Section \@ref(evaluation-criteria)).

## Validation of each method on observed events {#validation-contrast}

```{r all-methods-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 10, fig.cap = "The fitted curves from each method for six contrasting observed events, the black lines (earliest and latest peak, shortest and longest duration, and the flattest and sharpest peaks)."}
plot_all_methods()
```

```{r residuals-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "The residuals against standardised time for each method, where grey is the observed events and the coloured lines are the average. The five averages are compared in the bottom right panel."}
plot_all_residuals()
```

The polynomial method fits a single peak that is low and broad, so misses sharp and multi-peak events (Figure \@ref(fig:all-methods-plot)), and it also drifts at the ends of each event. Its residuals in Figure \@ref(fig:residuals-all) reflect this, being positive around the peak and negative on either side of it. The B-spline method has the same problem at the peak but follows the recession closely, with residuals close to zero after $u \approx 0.6$, whereas the gamma-type method fits poorly overall, since each curve can only have a single peak and must have the same baseflow at both ends.

PCA reproduces single-peak events well and multi-peak events closely, although it does underestimate some of the smaller peaks in the latter. Its residuals are small throughout, with the largest on the rising limb. Wavelets are similarly accurate but show unrealistic dips, because every event keeps the same detail coefficients, as well as deviations at the ends caused by the periodic boundary. The residuals are correlated over time, but this is not a concern here because the fits are only used as a basis rather than for inference.

## Accuracy and fitness for purpose {#cmp-accuracy}

```{r cmp-main, echo=FALSE}
kable(cmp_main_tbl, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrrr",
      col.names = c("Method", "$K$", "Inputs", "In-sample", "Held-out", "Held-out (\\% of peak)",
                    "Peak (m$^3$/s)", "Timing (h)", "Volume (\\%)", "Neg.", "Max $|r|$"),
      caption = "Comparison of SEPA's approach and the five methods at their chosen number of parameters, where errors are average absolute values over extreme flow events, in real units.") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 3, "RMSE (m$^3$/s)" = 3, "Held-out errors" = 3,
                     "Parameter behaviour" = 2), escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "HOLD_position"), font_size = 9) %>%
  footnote(general = paste0(
    "In the columns, $K$ is the number of shape parameters, and Inputs is the number of emulator inputs. ",
    "The held-out errors come from leave-one-out validation for SEPA, PCA and wavelets, while the polynomial, B-spline and gamma-type methods fit each event separately, so their held-out and in-sample errors are the same. ",
    "In the final columns, Neg. counts the events whose held-out curve has negative flow, and Max $|r|$ is the largest absolute correlation between shape parameters across events. For each column, the best value is shown in bold."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

```{r cmp-features, echo=FALSE}
kable(cmp_feat_tbl, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrr",
      col.names = c("Method", "Peak (m$^3$/s)", "Volume (\\%)", "90th pct.", "Worst",
                    "Duration (h)", "Volume (Mm$^3$)", "Volume bias (Mm$^3$)",
                    "Rising", "Falling"),
      caption = "Event-relevant features and worst-case performance of each method, based on held-out predictions.") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Bias" = 2, "RMSE across events (m$^3$/s)" = 2,
                     "Above threshold" = 3, "RMSE by limb (m$^3$/s)" = 2), escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "HOLD_position"), font_size = 9) %>%
  footnote(general = paste0(
    "Here, positive bias indicates overestimation, while Duration and Volume above threshold are mean ",
    "absolute errors, and the rising and falling limbs are split at the observed peak."),
    threeparttable = TRUE)
```

```{r cmp-distribution, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Held-out errors for every extreme flow event under each method, shown on a log scale. Each box covers the middle 50\\% of events, and the individual points mark events with unusually large errors."}
per_event_long_plot
```

All of the methods achieve a lower RMSE than SEPA's approach (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-main)), and the improvement is largest for PCA and wavelets, which bring it down from `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ to `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_wav)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, or roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa / cmp_text$rmse_pca)` and `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa / cmp_text$rmse_wav)` times lower. Because SEPA matches the peak by construction, its errors come from the shape of the hydrograph, and since it gives every event the same duration it overstates the volume of some events and understates others. Hence, its volume error averages `r sprintf("%.0f", S("SEPA (average shape)", "volume_out"))`\% even though its overall bias is only `r sprintf("%+.0f", cmp_text$volume_sepa)`\% (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-features)). The polynomial and B-spline methods both underestimate the peak, with peak errors of `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$peak_poly)` and `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$peak_bspline)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, and they each give negative flow in `r S("Polynomial", "neg_events")` events. Their flattened peaks, along with the single-peak form of the gamma-type method, also mean that the timing of the maximum is out by between `r sprintf("%.1f", min(sapply(c("Gamma-type", "Polynomial", "B-spline"), S, col = "timing_out")))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", max(sapply(c("Gamma-type", "Polynomial", "B-spline"), S, col = "timing_out")))` hours.

Wavelets give the lowest errors on most metrics, although they produce negative flow in `r S("Wavelets", "neg_events")` events, compared with `r S("PCA", "neg_events")` for PCA. PCA's 90th-percentile error of `r sprintf("%.1f", S("PCA", "rmse_p90"))` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ is still less than half of SEPA's average error (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-features), Figure \@ref(fig:cmp-distribution)). Also, its RMSE only rises from `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca_in)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ when events are held out, which suggests that its basis generalises well to new events.

## Parsimony {#cmp-parsimony}

```{r cmp-tradeoff, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Accuracy against number of shape parameters for every setting tried in Section 3. The circled points are the chosen settings and the dashed line is SEPA's approach, which uses leave-one-out to calculate the errors."}
tradeoff_long_plot
```

Each shape parameter adds an emulator input, and with it more runs of the slow inundation model. So, we consider the methods at the same number of parameters, and we find that PCA usually gives the lowest errors (Figure \@ref(fig:cmp-tradeoff)), except for volume error, where it is in line with the other methods. In particular, comparing at $K =$ `r ncol(wav_params)`, PCA's held-out RMSE is `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$pca_at_wav_K)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ against wavelets' `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_wav)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, which suggests that wavelets' lower error comes from extra parameters, not a better basis.

In terms of correlations, PCA scores are uncorrelated by construction and gamma-type parameters are weakly correlated, up to `r sprintf("%.2f", S("Gamma-type", "max_cor"))`. On the other hand, polynomial coefficients are near-collinear, up to `r sprintf("%.2f", S("Polynomial", "max_cor"))`, while B-spline and wavelet coefficients reach `r sprintf("%.2f", S("B-spline", "max_cor"))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", S("Wavelets", "max_cor"))`. This is important for Section \@ref(uncertainty), where we fit a joint distribution for the shape parameters.

## Evaluating the differences {#cmp-paired}

```{r cmp-paired, echo=FALSE}
kable(select(paired_tbl, -Comparison), format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
                      align = "lrrrr",
                      col.names = c("Metric", "Mean difference", "95\\% bootstrap CI",
                                    "Events where first is better (\\%)", "Wilcoxon $p$"),
                      caption = "Comparison of held-out absolute errors between two methods over the same events, where a negative difference means the first-named method has smaller errors.") %>%
  pack_rows(index = table(paired_tbl$Comparison)) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 9)
```

From Table \@ref(tab:cmp-paired), the bootstrap confidence intervals and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show the differences are real. PCA and wavelets beat SEPA on RMSE and volume error for `r sprintf("%.0f", min(sapply(vs_sepa, function(cm) c(pr_val(cm, "rmse", "first_better"), pr_val(cm, "volume_error", "first_better")))))`\% of events, although SEPA's peak errors are slightly smaller, by under 1 $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, as it matches the peak by construction. PCA also beats the B-spline on peak error for `r sprintf("%.0f", pr_val("PCA minus B-spline", "peak_error", "first_better"))`\% of events. Wavelets beat PCA on RMSE for `r sprintf("%.0f", pr_val("Wavelets minus PCA", "rmse", "first_better"))`\% of events, but the latter has the smaller peak error for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 - pr_val("Wavelets minus PCA", "peak_error", "first_better"))`\%. Their RMSE difference of `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(cmp_text$wav_minus_pca))` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ is small next to their gain of about `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa - cmp_text$rmse_pca)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ over SEPA.

## Methods carried forward {#cmp-synthesis}

```{r cmp-synthesis, echo=FALSE}
kable(synthesis, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Method", "Accuracy (held-out RMSE)", "Event features", "Unusual events",
                    "Shape parameters", "Parameter behaviour", "Physical validity",
                    "Interpretability"),
      caption = "Summary of the comparison against the three criteria, where the two methods carried forward to the uncertainty analysis are in bold.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "1.6cm") %>%
  column_spec(c(2:5, 7), width = "1.4cm") %>%   # 8 columns fit a 16cm text width
  column_spec(6, width = "1.8cm") %>%
  column_spec(8, width = "1.8cm") %>%
  row_spec(which(synthesis$Method %in% c("PCA", "Wavelets")), bold = TRUE)
```

Following our comparison, we eliminate SEPA's approach, which cannot capture differences in duration or volume, as well as the polynomial and B-spline methods, which erode the peak and give negative flows, and the gamma-type method, which, though the most parsimonious and interpretable, cannot represent multi-peak events and has `r sprintf("%.1f", S("Gamma-type", "rmse_out") / S("PCA", "rmse_out"))` times PCA's RMSE. We move forward with PCA, which has fewer, uncorrelated parameters, and wavelets, which have the lowest error. Our choice between them depends on their ability to simulate new events in Section \@ref(uncertainty).

# Uncertainty analysis {#uncertainty}

We now model how the PCA and wavelet shape parameters vary between events, so that new hydrographs can be simulated and propagated through an emulator.

## Distribution and dependencies of the shape parameters

As peak flow, duration and peak position are held separately from the shape parameters, we first check whether the two sets are dependent.

```{r dependence, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Spearman correlations between each shape parameter and the standardisation parameters (peak flow, duration and peak position), for the PCA scores (PC1--PC6) and the wavelet smooth (S1--S8) and detail (D1--D5) coefficients. Red indicates negative, blue indicates positive, and bold is a magnitude of at least 0.5."}
plot_dependence()
```

Some of the correlations in Figure \@ref(fig:dependence) are moderate to strong, in particular, $-0.80$ between PC2 and peak position and $-0.74$ between S5 and peak position. This motivates fitting a conditional scheme, otherwise we may pair shapes with sizes and timings that do not actually occur together. To explore which scheme, we regress the shape parameters on the standardisation parameters and model the residuals.

```{r param-qq, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Normal Q-Q plots of the residuals of each shape parameter after regressing it on peak flow, duration and peak position. The PCA scores (PC1-PC6) are blue and on the top row, while the wavelet smooth (S1-S8) and detail (D1-D5) coefficients are pink and on the bottom two rows."}
plot_residual_qq()
```

Figure \@ref(fig:param-qq) suggests that the residuals are approximately Normal through the centre of their distributions, but that several depart from Normality in the tails. In particular, PC2 and PC4-PC6 have heavy lower tails, while for the wavelets, S1-S3 are right-skewed and D1, D2, D4 and D5 have heavy tails, particularly in the upper tail. Therefore, we fit a conditional multivariate Normal distribution alongside a conditional smoothed bootstrap, which relies less on Normality. Figure \@ref(fig:residual-fitted) plots the same residuals against their fitted values, to check whether their spread is constant.

```{r residual-fitted, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "The residuals against fitted values from the regression of each shape parameter on the standardisation parameters. The PCA scores (PC1-PC6) are blue and on the top row, while the wavelet smooth (S1-S8) and detail (D1-D5) coefficients are pink and on the bottom two rows."}
plot_residual_fitted()
```

## Statistical model and sampling scheme {#model}

Let $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i = (\theta_{i1}, \dots, \theta_{iK})^\top$ be the shape parameters for event $i$, either the PCA scores ($K = 6$) or the wavelet coefficients ($K = 13$), and $\mathbf{s}_i = (Q_i^{\text{peak}}, W_i, \tau_i)^\top$ its standardisation parameters. Both schemes regress the shape parameters on the standardisation parameters,

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\theta}_i = \boldsymbol{\beta}_0 + B\,\mathbf{s}_i + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i,
(\#eq:regression)
\end{equation}

where $B$ is a $K \times 3$ matrix of coefficients. Fitting this by least squares gives residuals $\hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_1, \dots, \hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_N$ with sample covariance $\hat{\Sigma}$, and a new event with standardisation parameters $\mathbf{s}^\ast$ has simulated shape parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}^\ast = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0 + \hat{B}\,\mathbf{s}^\ast + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast$. This assumes that the residual spread is the same for every $\mathbf{s}^\ast$, which Figure \@ref(fig:residual-fitted) supports for PCA, but not for the wavelet detail coefficients D1, D2 and D4, where the spread widens as the fitted value increases. The two schemes we consider differ only in how $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast$ is generated, and our conditional Normal model takes

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast \sim N_K(\mathbf{0}, \hat{\Sigma}).
(\#eq:cond-normal)
\end{equation}

In comparison, the conditional smoothed bootstrap takes

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast = \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_J + h\,\mathbf{z}}{\sqrt{1+h^2}}, \qquad J \sim \text{Uniform}\{1,\dots,N\}, \quad \mathbf{z} \sim N_K(\mathbf{0}, \hat{\Sigma}),
(\#eq:cond-boot)
\end{equation}

with $h = \big(4/((K+2)N)\big)^{1/(K+4)}$ [@silverman1986]. The bootstrap retains some of the heavy tails seen in Figure \@ref(fig:param-qq), although the Normal noise accounts for `r round(100 * noise_share_pca)`\% (PCA) and `r round(100 * noise_share_wav)`\% (wavelets) of the variance of the simulated residuals.

Finally, we turn $\boldsymbol{\theta}^\ast$ into a curve using Equation \@ref(eq:pca) for PCA or \@ref(eq:wavelet) for wavelets, and reverse the standardisation with $\mathbf{s}^\ast$.

## Evaluation criteria {#uncertainty-criteria}

To evaluate how well each combination of method and scheme simulates extreme flow events, we simulate $R =$ `r n_each` shapes for each event $i$ using its own standardisation parameters $\mathbf{s}_i$ and convert them to hydrographs $\hat{Q}_i^{(r)}(t_j)$. We then compare these with the observed hydrograph $Q_i(t_j)$ at the `r n_grid` time points of Section \@ref(standardising-the-hydrographs), and average over all events.

**Coverage:** The percentage of the observed hydrograph that falls within the simulated 90\% band,

\begin{equation}
\text{Coverage}_i = \frac{100}{`r n_grid`}\sum_{j} \mathbf{1}\big\{L_i(t_j) \le Q_i(t_j) \le U_i(t_j)\big\},
(\#eq:coverage)
\end{equation}

where $L_i(t_j)$ and $U_i(t_j)$ are the 5\% and 95\% quantiles of the simulated flows at $t_j$.

**CRPS:** This is a measure of the accuracy and spread of simulations [@gneitingraftery2007], where lower is better, and it is in $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$,

\begin{equation}
\text{CRPS}_i = \frac{1}{`r n_grid`}\sum_{j}\left( \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r} \big|\hat{Q}_i^{(r)}(t_j) - Q_i(t_j)\big| - \frac{1}{2R^2}\sum_{r}\sum_{r'} \big|\hat{Q}_i^{(r)}(t_j) - \hat{Q}_i^{(r')}(t_j)\big| \right),
(\#eq:crps)
\end{equation}

**Physical validity:** We also want to understand whether the simulations produce realistic hydrograph shapes. We consider the percentage of simulated standardised curves that have negative flow, or that rise more than 1\% above the peak.

## Validating the simulations {#uncertainty-validating-sim}

Before simulating new events, we check whether each combination's simulations are consistent with real events that are not used to fit it.

```{r out-of-sample, echo=FALSE}
kable(out_of_sample[, -1], format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("", "Coverage (\\%)", "CRPS (m$^3$/s)", "Negative flow (\\%)", "Above peak (\\%)"),
      escape = FALSE,
      caption = paste0("We conduct leave-one-out validation, where each event is left out of the fit and 200 curves are simulated with its own peak flow, duration and peak position. The criteria of coverage, negative flow and above peak are measured on simulated curves, so they do not apply to SEPA's single fixed shape, for which the CRPS is the mean absolute error.")) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 9) %>%
  pack_rows("SEPA", 1, 1) %>%
  pack_rows("PCA", 2, 3) %>%
  pack_rows("Wavelets", 4, 5)
```

```{r held-out-bands, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="The 90\\% band from each combination, with 200 simulated hydrographs for three contrasting extreme flow events, (events 40, 60 and 70: the latest peak, the longest duration and the flattest peak). Each is left out of the fit, and the observed hydrograph is displayed in black."}
plot_held_out_bands()
```

We observe that each combination improves on SEPA's approach, reducing CRPS by at least `r floor(100 * (1 - max(out_of_sample$crps[-1]) / out_of_sample$crps[1]))`%. Comparing between methods and schemes, the CRPS values are almost identical, so we compare them on the other criteria.

The coverage is below 90\% for every combination, and Figure \@ref(fig:held-out-bands) shows that observed hydrographs mainly leave the band at multi-peaks. PCA and wavelets have similar coverage, but more wavelet curves are physically invalid, with `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("Wavelets", "Conditional bootstrap", "above_peak"))`\% rising above their peak under the bootstrap, against `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "above_peak"))`\% for PCA. For PCA, the Normal has marginally better coverage and CRPS than the bootstrap, but the bootstrap produces fewer curves with negative flow (`r sprintf("%.1f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "negative"))`\% against `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("PCA", "Conditional Normal", "negative"))`\%).

## Simulating new extreme flow events {#uncertainty-sim}

We refit each combination to every event and simulate `r n_sim` new standardised hydrographs, each using the peak flow, duration and peak position of a randomly chosen observed event.

```{r fan-charts, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap=paste0("The median, 25-75\\% and 5-95\\% bands of the ", n_sim, " simulated standardised hydrographs for each combination, where the observed events are in grey.")}
plot_fan_charts()
```

We observe that each method and scheme gives very similar overall shapes and bands (Figure \@ref(fig:fan-charts)), with most observed events lying within the 90\% band, the main exceptions being multi-peaks on the recession, which is in line with Section \@ref(uncertainty-validating-sim). We notice that the upper edges rise slightly above the peak, more so for wavelets, and under the Normal scheme the lower edges reach zero near the start, which the bootstrap avoids.

To directly tie our analysis to flood risk, we also consider the total volume of a typical extreme flow event, on which the extent of a flood strongly depends.

```{r volumes, echo=FALSE}
kable(volume_table, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("", "5\\%", "Median", "95\\%"), escape = FALSE,
      caption = paste0("Total volume (million m$^3$) of an event with the median peak flow (",
                       round(typical["peak_flow"]), " m$^3$/s), duration (", round(typical["duration"]),
                       " h) and peak position (", sprintf("%.2f", typical["peak_position"]), "), ",
                       "comparing SEPA's single shape against 1000 simulated shapes from each combination.")) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 9)
```

Our combinations give medians of `r sprintf("%.1f", min(volume_table$median[-1]))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(volume_table$median[-1]))` million $\text{m}^3$, with 90\% bands spanning `r sprintf("%.1f", min(volume_table$lower, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(volume_table$upper, na.rm = TRUE))` million $\text{m}^3$ (Table \@ref(tab:volumes)). If we keep only the physically valid PCA bootstrap curves this barely changes, giving `r sprintf("%.1f", pca_boot_valid_volume$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", pca_boot_valid_volume$upper)` million $\text{m}^3$. SEPA's single value of `r sprintf("%.1f", volume_table$median[1])` million $\text{m}^3$ is close to the simulated medians, but it gives no representation of how much flood volume can change because of an event's shape alone.

## Other uncertainties

We first analyse sampling error, (how far our events depend on the `r nrow(Y)` events we observed). We resample them with replacement `r n_boot` times, each time refitting both the shape method and the distribution and record the edges of the simulated 90\% band.

```{r sampling, echo=FALSE}
kable(sampling_table, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("", "Band width", "SD of lower edge", "SD of upper edge"),
      caption = paste0("Width of the simulated 90\\% band and the standard deviation of its edges across ",
                 n_boot, " refits to resampled events, both given as fractions of peak flow."),
      escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 9)
```

The band has an average width of around `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(sampling_table$band_width))` of the peak flow, while the standard deviation of its edges between refits is only `r sprintf("%.3f", min(sampling_table[, c("lower_sd", "upper_sd")]))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(sampling_table[, c("lower_sd", "upper_sd")]))`, around `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(unlist(sampling_table[, c("lower_sd", "upper_sd")])) / mean(sampling_table$band_width))`\% of its width (Table \@ref(tab:sampling), Figure \@ref(fig:sampling-bands)). Therefore, sampling variability is small relative to the simulated uncertainty, and it is almost identical across combinations, even for wavelets' `r ncol(wav_params)` parameters.

```{r sampling-bands, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Edges of the simulated 90\\% band from 100 refits to resampled events, for each combination."}
plot_sampling_bands()
```

Finally, there remain uncertainties that are unquantified, which we outline in Table \@ref(tab:other-uncertainty)

Table: (\#tab:other-uncertainty) Uncertainties not quantified in this analysis.

| Source | Likely effect | How it could be addressed |
|:--------------------------------|:------------------------|:----------------------------|
| The 65 m$^3$/s threshold and the independence criteria used to pick out events | A different threshold would give a different set of events to model | Rerun the analysis with other thresholds and compare the results |
| Errors in the rating curve at high flows, and the Estimated readings we kept (2.5\% of the record) | Peak flows and shapes may be slightly wrong | Use SEPA's own estimates of rating-curve error, and check whether dropping the Estimated readings changes anything |
| Changes in climate or land use over the 25 years | Events in the past may not look like events in the future | Check whether the shape parameters drift over time |
| Our choice of PCA and of $K = 6$ components | Some of the variation in real shapes is missing from the simulations | Compare results for other methods and values of $K$ |
| Peak flows larger than any we have observed | The regression has to extrapolate, so the shapes of the rarest events are less reliable | Look at the simulated shapes for very large peak flows before using them |
| Uneven spread in wavelet coefficients D1, D2 and D4 (Figure \@ref(fig:residual-fitted)) | The wavelet simulations get the uncertainty in shape slightly wrong | Let the spread depend on the fitted value |

# Recommendation and emulator application

## Recommendation {#recommendation}

We recommend that SEPA represents hydrograph shape using PCA with `r k_chosen` principal component scores, alongside peak flow, duration and peak position, and simulates new shapes using the conditional smoothed bootstrap (Equations \@ref(eq:regression) and \@ref(eq:cond-boot)).

PCA offers substantial improvement on SEPA's approach, reducing the held-out RMSE by `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$red_pca)`\% and its volume error from `r sprintf("%.1f", S("SEPA (average shape)", "volume_out"))`\% to `r sprintf("%.2f", S("PCA", "volume_out"))`\% (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-main)). Wavelets reconstruct the observed events slightly more accurately, but their advantage comes from extra parameters rather than a better basis (Section \@ref(cmp-parsimony)). With $K =$ `r k_chosen` rather than `r ncol(wav_params)`, PCA needs only `r S("PCA", "inputs")` emulator inputs compared with `r S("Wavelets", "inputs")` for wavelets, reducing the number of inundation model runs required, and its joint distribution needs `r choose(k_chosen, 2)` rather than `r choose(ncol(wav_params), 2)` correlations. When simulating new events, both methods are almost identical in terms of coverage and CRPS, but PCA's curves are more physically valid, with `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "above_peak"))`\% rising above their peak compared with `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("Wavelets", "Conditional bootstrap", "above_peak"))`\% for wavelets, and only PCA satisfies the constant-spread assumption (Figure \@ref(fig:residual-fitted)).

Comparing the bootstrap to the conditional Normal, the Normal has marginally better coverage and CRPS for PCA, but we prefer the bootstrap because it produces fewer curves with negative flow, `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "negative"))`\% against `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("PCA", "Conditional Normal", "negative"))`\%. Furthermore, the bootstrap relies less on Normality, which is important given the heavy tails we observed in Figure \@ref(fig:param-qq).

The PCA method has limitations, the most immediate being that it still produces `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "negative"))`\% of curves with negative flow and `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "above_peak"))`\% that rise above their peak. SEPA could discard these and draw replacements, although this would truncate the distribution and was not done in our validation (Table \@ref(tab:out-of-sample)), or it could instead rescale each curve to its own maximum. The `r k_chosen` components also do not fully capture multi-peak events, so the uncertainty in shape is probably slightly understated, which partly explains why coverage of `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "coverage"))`\% falls short of the 90\% we aimed for. Finally, because the bootstrap resamples residuals from only `r nrow(Y)` events, it cannot generate shapes much more extreme than those we have already observed, and so may miss the rarest and most impactful events.

## Emulator application {#emulator}

**Collecting the data to fit the emulator:** SEPA selects its training inputs by choosing a few hundred combinations of the `r S("PCA", "inputs")` inputs using an experimental statistical design [@wilson2026lec3]. Each combinations is then turned into a hydrograph using Equation \@ref(eq:pca) and reversing the standardisation done previously. This is then run through the flood inundation model, and an emulator is fitted to the pairs of inputs and outputs and checked against a separate set of runs withheld from the fitting process. This can then be used to approximate the flood inundation model at a fraction of the cost.

**Using the emulator to explore uncertainty in flood inundation:**
Following this, SEPA can use our conditional smoothed bootstrap to simulate new extreme flow events, in practice drawing peak flows from its existing extreme value distribution rather than resampling observed events like we did. Since emulators are much faster than the inundation model, thousands of these events can be passed through giving a full distribution of flood depths or extents that reflects parametric uncertainty (uncertainty in both the size and shape of the hydrograph). We also have functional uncertainty, (uncertainty in the emulator's own prediction) and structural uncertainty, (the structural discrepancy that remains between the inundation model and real flooding, and between our statistical model and the real variation in hydrograph shape) these should also be added to this distribution [@wilson2026lec3]. The structural uncertainty being clear as our simulated 90\% bands contain only around `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "coverage"))`\%  of the observed hydrographs.
